newsitem.title: USA: NATO expansion tops Clinton-Yeltsin summit agenda.
newsitem.headline: NATO expansion tops Clinton-Yeltsin summit agenda.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's main goal at a U.S.-Russian summit in Helsinki next week is convincing a sceptical Boris Yeltsin NATO's planned eastward expansion will stabilise Europe and poses no threat to Russia.

It's a tall order for the U.S. president. Yeltsin, just returning to the world stage after being sidelined by illness for more than six months, has warned repeatedly that bringing Russia's neighbours into the Western alliance would be viewed by the Kremlin as an unfriendly act.
At a news conference last Friday, Clinton said he could understand Russian sensitivities since "we were never invaded by Napolean and Hitler, and they were."

"I expect that the Helsinki meeting will be positive. But you should understand that this is a tough debate and that they have reasons in their own psyche and circumstances that make it a difficult one," he said.

The United States and its NATO allies will meet in Madrid in July to decide which former communist Warsaw Pact nations will get the first invitations to join NATO. Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to get the nod.

Clinton and the Russian president are expected to meet over dinner in the Finnish capital on March 19 but the bulk of their talks will take place the next day at the secluded seaside residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari.

A U.S. official said Yeltsin seemed to be fully recovered from heart surgery and a bout of pneumonia and was thought to be in shape physically to engage in extensive give-and-take. "We won't keep him up late," the official joked.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said that in addition to NATO expansion the two presidents would focus on arms control and Russia's transformation to a market economy. He said Clinton would pass along U.S. ideas for structural and legal reforms in Russia "which would allow for greater capital formation and encourage more outside investment."

The official said Clinton would also offer ideas about how foreign assistance to Russia can be used more effectively and perhaps promise Yeltsin "some new money." He refused to discuss a dollar figure.

Another summit talking point will be Russian membership in the club of big industrial democracies now called the Group of Seven. "You'll see a further enhancement of Russian membership in time for the Denver Summit in June. What it will be will be worked out this spring," the official said.

Clinton and Yeltsin will discuss arms control questions such as how to interpret a 25-year-old anti-ballistic missile (ABM) treaty and what follow-on limits on strategic nuclear weapons should be put on the negotiating table once the Russian parliament ratifies the START-2 treaty.
The 1972 ABM treaty is a summit topic because the United States wants to establish a clear understanding that it does not prohibit development of a theatre missile defence.
NATO expansion will clearly dominate the summit, however.

Asked how Clinton would try to overcome Yeltsin's fears of encirclement, an official familiar with the president's case said he would argue that NATO "is not an encircling alliance but a cooperative infrastructure and that Russia too can take advantage of it to provide stability in Europe.

"Even the prospect of NATO expansion is a stabilising influence -- it has brought agreements between Hungary and Romania, Hungary and Slovakia and the Czech Republic and Germany. People in Central Europe are putting old differences behind them," the official said.
Clinton and Yeltsin will also discuss a formal connection, or charter, between NATO and Russia.

To set the stage for the Helsinki talks, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov will visit Washington this weekend. He will hold a working luncheon with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright at the State Department on Saturday and meet with Clinton at the White House on Monday.
